item.title: Forget the gym: A 30-second test may be one of the best indicators of longevity
item.description: A certified personal trainer reveals the benchmarks for the 30-second chair stand test and exercises that can improve lower body strength and fall risk.
item.content:encoded:
As more Americans prioritize staying mobile and independent as they age, experts are pointing to a surprisingly simple measure of health.

The number of times a person can rise from a chair in 30 seconds can be an indicator of lower-body strength, which is closely linked to mobility, functional fitness and healthy aging.

Interest in the test appears to be growing, with online searches for "sit to stand exercise" up 287% over the past three months, according to Google Trends analysis.

JANE SEYMOUR, 75, SHARES HOW SHE APPROACHES AGING WITH VITALITY: 'BEST I CAN BE'

The CDC's Stopping Elderly Accidents, Deaths & Injuries (STEADI) program states that the purpose of the 30-second chair stand test is to assess leg strength and endurance, with below-average scores indicating increased fall risk.

Bruno Pontes, an ACSM- and AFAA-certified personal trainer at Muscle Booster in California, shared what the sit-to-stand test actually measures and why experts consider it a strong indicator of fitness.

Nick Schofield, a tactical athlete physical coach in the U.K., also provided a video demonstration of the exercise for Muscle Booster.

"What makes this test a great measure of fitness is that it simulates the everyday movement of getting up and down from a chair, compared to machine-based strength tests, which instead isolate muscle groups," Pontes told Fox News Digital.

'FIT MOM' DID 'EVERYTHING RIGHT' — THEN A COLON CANCER DIAGNOSIS CHANGED HER LIFE

"The sit-to-stand test is an excellent indicator of lower-body strength, muscular endurance, balance and mobility," Pontes said. It is also commonly used by healthcare professionals to help assess fall risk in older adults.

While there are several iterations of the sit-to-stand test, the 30-second chair stand test is the go-to exercise endorsed by public health organizations like the CDC, the expert noted.

The sit-to-stand test is easy to perform at home, Pontes said, as the only thing needed is a sturdy chair. He outlined the following steps.

LOW TESTOSTERONE? HEGSETH SPARKS CONVERSATION AS DOCTORS REVEAL WARNING SIGNS EVERY MAN SHOULD KNOW

"As an important note, anyone with significant balance problems, recent surgery, severe joint pain or cardiovascular concerns should consult a healthcare professional before performing the test," Pontes advised.

What is seen as a "good" score varies from person to person and is dependent on a number of factors, including age and gender, Pontes said.

"However, the following benchmarks are good to aim for to measure your lower-body strength," he added. These benchmarks are based on how many full stands can be completed in 30 seconds from a standard-height chair.

"It is important not to obsess over the number you achieve — the focus should be on the ease of movement and making daily functions easier," Pontes said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"If rising from a chair becomes easier over time, that's a great indicator that lower-body strength and functional fitness are improving," he went on. "If you fall below the target number, don’t worry — there are many different exercises you can implement into your daily routine to help strengthen your lower body."

The following exercises can be executed at home to help improve your sit-to-stand performance, according to Pontes. These moves help to build strength in the quads, hamstrings, glutes and calves.

Squats

"Squats help to build strength primarily in the quadriceps and glutes, while also engaging the hamstrings and core," Pontes told Fox News Digital. "They are also a great exercise for seniors, as they place limited amounts of stress on your hips and spine."

Squats can be performed by standing with the feet shoulder-width apart and lowering the hips back and down into a seated position. Be sure to keep the back straight and chest up.

Lunges

"These low-impact exercises can help identify any strength imbalances that may be affecting mobility and stability, as each leg works independently," Pontes said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

To perform a lunge, stand with the feet shoulder-width apart and step forward with one leg, creating a right angle at the knee. The front knee should sit directly over the ankle/heel and should not extend past the toes.

Hold this position briefly before pushing through the heel on the front foot to engage the glutes and return to the starting position, then repeat for the other leg.

Calf raises

"Calf raises help keep the calf muscles strong and functional as we age, to support everyday, functional movements," Pontes said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Stand with the feet hip-width apart, keeping an upright posture and engaging the core. Slowly push through the balls of the feet to raise the heels off the floor as high as possible. Pause briefly at the top, then lower the heels back down to the ground with control.

As people age, they become more susceptible to sarcopenia, the gradual loss of muscle mass and strength over time, according to Pontes. This can make routine activities more difficult and increases the risk of injury.

"Lower-body strength plays a vital role in maintaining independence because it supports many of the movements we rely on every day, such as climbing stairs, getting up from chairs, carrying groceries and walking confidently," the fitness expert noted.

Maintaining strength in the legs and hips helps to preserve mobility and lower the risk of falls and injury, Pontes said.

"This mobility helps enable people to remain active and keep moving freely through their later years."

item.title: Attorney who defended DC sniper says Kohberger faces 'monumental uphill battle' undoing guilty plea
item.description: A criminal defense attorney explains why Bryan Kohberger's effort to undo his University of Idaho murders guilty plea faces two significant legal hurdles.
item.content:encoded:
Bryan Kohberger faces a "monumental uphill battle" in his effort to withdraw his guilty plea in the murders of four University of Idaho students, according to an attorney who represented D.C. sniper Lee Boyd Malvo and once helped another client successfully withdraw a guilty plea before winning an acquittal.

Mark Petrovich, who represented Malvo in post-conviction proceedings in Virginia and has decades of criminal defense experience, told Fox News Digital that defendants rarely succeed in withdrawing guilty pleas after sentencing, even in cases involving claims that they were unaware of potentially exculpatory evidence before entering the plea.

He cautioned against drawing direct comparisons between Malvo's post-conviction litigation and Kohberger's effort to withdraw his guilty plea. Malvo's appeals stemmed from changes in constitutional law governing juvenile sentencing, while Kohberger is attempting to undo a plea agreement he entered as an adult after avoiding the death penalty.

KAYLEE GONCALVES' MOTHER SAYS FAMILY READY FOR TRIAL AFTER BRYAN KOHBERGER SEEKS TO WITHDRAW GUILTY PLEA

"It's a monumental uphill battle," Petrovich said. "First of all, getting the judge to allow you to withdraw the plea, and then second of all to winning any new proceeding, because there's a lot against you."

Kohberger pleaded guilty in July 2025 to the stabbing deaths of University of Idaho students Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle, Madison Mogen and Kaylee Goncalves in Moscow, Idaho, in November 2022. He was sentenced to four consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole after accepting a plea agreement that spared him from the death penalty.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

In recent court filings, Kohberger claimed he was pressured into accepting the plea agreement, did not fully understand potentially exculpatory evidence before pleading guilty and was misled about the conditions he would face while incarcerated.

IDAHO MURDERS: NEW BOOK ON KOHBERGER REVEALS PREVIOUSLY UNSEEN EVIDENCE, CLAIMS SHEATH COULD BE INADMISSIBLE

He contends those factors undermined the voluntariness of his decision to plead guilty.

Petrovich said he once represented a client who sought to withdraw a guilty plea before sentencing. A judge granted the request, the case proceeded to trial and the client was acquitted, but he said Kohberger's circumstances are fundamentally different because he has already been sentenced.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"You can't wait until after you're sentenced and see what the consequences of the plea are and then change your plea," Petrovich said. "It's going to be a very, very difficult burden to overcome."

ALEX MURDAUGH MURDER SAGA LANDS RIGHT BACK WHERE IT STARTED BEFORE NEXT LOWCOUNTRY COURTROOM BATTLE

Petrovich said Kohberger would face two significant hurdles even if a judge allowed him to withdraw his plea.

One would be convincing jurors after previously admitting guilt under oath.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Even if a judge allowed Kohberger to withdraw his plea, Petrovich said jurors would almost certainly learn he had already admitted guilt, creating another significant obstacle at trial.

SEND US A TIP

"One thing that's important is that you still can't hide from the jury the fact that you said under oath that you're guilty," Petrovich said. "Even if you withdraw, then you have to explain that ... if you're going to get anywhere with any kind of jury finding."

Petrovich also questioned whether Kohberger's attorneys would have advised him to accept a plea agreement without first reviewing the evidence disclosed during discovery.

GOT A TIP?

He noted that defense attorneys handling capital cases typically spend years reviewing discovery before recommending whether a client should plead guilty.

"The attorneys on the case ... were intimately familiar with the evidence and the information that was provided to them by law enforcement and prosecution," Petrovich said. "I'm sure they knew all about everything. If they encouraged him or if there was a discussion and a plea was decided on, I'm sure it was for good reason."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Kohberger's case is not the first involving a notorious killer who later sought to undo a guilty plea.

James Earl Ray pleaded guilty in 1969 to assassinating the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. to avoid a potential death sentence. Three days after entering his guilty plea, Ray sought to withdraw it, arguing he had been pressured into confessing. He spent the rest of his life trying to undo the plea but died in prison in 1998 without ever receiving the jury trial he sought.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

Serial killer Clifton Bloomfield unsuccessfully sought to withdraw guilty pleas after admitting to five murders in New Mexico to avoid capital punishment. Washington serial killer Robert Lee Yates Jr. also challenged his plea agreement after admitting to murdering 13 women, but courts ultimately rejected both efforts.

Kohberger's plea agreement spared him from facing a capital trial and ended years of pretrial litigation in one of the country's most closely watched murder prosecutions.

Petrovich said that history, combined with the years of discovery and plea negotiations leading up to Kohberger's agreement, makes the effort to withdraw it especially difficult.

item.title: CNN's Dana Bash spars with RFK Jr over vaccine efficacy, demands he 'look into the camera' and push vaccines
item.description: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. clashed with CNN host Dana Bash over measles vaccine hesitancy after accusing her of committing "press malpractice" on air.
item.content:encoded:
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sparred with CNN host Dana Bash over the rise in measles cases in the United States as well as vaccine efficacy on Sunday's "State of the Union."

Though the interview grew heated after Kennedy accused Bash of committing "press malpractice" based on what he said was a failure to challenge public health authorities during the COVID pandemic, Kennedy and Bash's contention continued after Bash asked him about the record number of measles cases and whether he accepts "some responsibility."

"Absolutely not," Kennedy said. "First of all, this is an international outbreak. So, we're doing better at handling it than any country in the world. Mexico has 15 times the amount of measles per capita that we have. Canada has four times the amount of measles. England has two times the amount of measles. Did I cause those measles outbreaks?"

RFK JR ACCUSES NYT OF PUBLISHING 'HIT PIECE' SOURCED BY 'DISGRUNTLED' EMPLOYEES HE PURGED

Bash suggested he bears some responsibility as the "most famous vaccine skeptic on the planet," though Kennedy countered that former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Director Dr. Anthony Fauci himself has said in his private diaries that COVID lockdowns were more responsible for children not being vaccinated for measles.

The CNN host, however, continued to demand Kennedy use his position to advocate for people to take the measles vaccine.

"What I want you to do is please use your bully pulpit to, right now, as we're getting close to back to school, say — are you willing to say to parents who have not vaccinated their kids that they should vaccinate their kids for measles because it is safe, and it will help them save their children's lives?" Bash asked.

"I tell people on my websites, my public..." Kennedy began.

"Right now. Look into the camera," Bash interrupted.

RFK JR WAS RIGHT TO CONFRONT CNN OVER FAUCI COVERAGE, SAY NETWORK WAS 'SCARING PEOPLE' DURING COVID-19

"I will say it right now, that people, parents should get their children vaccinated for measles. A measles vaccine is effective. It stops measles in about 97% of the cases. So, people should get vaccinated," Kennedy said.

Bash went on to ask Kennedy about efforts to investigate connections between vaccines and autism. While Kennedy was explaining his position, he stopped to call out Bash for "rolling [her] eyes" at the issue.

"I don't want to have you use our air to say this," Bash said.

Bash then accused Kennedy of promoting vaccine skepticism by suggesting vaccines could cause autism, despite his previous support for the measles and MMR vaccine. Kennedy remarked that Bash appeared "flustered."

"I am frustrated. The reason I'm frustrated is because I… you are the HHS secretary, and you are talking about things that lead to vaccine hesitancy in this country. And it is something that causes problems for people when there is not anything..." Bash said.

RFK JR SAYS FAUCI PRIORITIZED 'GETTING ON TV' OVER PUBLIC HEALTH AFTER REVEALING DIARY RELEASE

"Let me ask you something. Do you see your job as ending vaccine hesitancy, or do you see your job as telling the truth to the American people?" Kennedy asked.

"I see my job as telling the truth," Bash responded.

CNN defended Bash's performance in a statement to Fox News Digital after it aired.

"Dana Bash is a veteran journalist who conducted a newsmaking interview with Secretary Kennedy in which he stated that he supports parents getting their children vaccinated against measles and addressed President Trump’s push for further study into autism and vaccines," a CNN spokesperson said.

"Asking tough, substantive questions to those in power is the job of every journalist, and Dana did hers incredibly well today. We stand behind Dana, her reporting, and CNN’s overall coverage of the COVID-19 pandemic," the spokesperson added.

CNN stood by the statement when reached for further comment.

item.title: JUAN WILLIAMS: My nephew returned from space with a message America needs
item.description: NASA astronaut Chris Williams, nephew of Fox News contributor Juan Williams, returned to Earth after eight months on the ISS, completing spacewalks and 3,856 orbits.
item.content:encoded:
In one of this year’s most popular movies, "Project Hail Mary," there’s no happy ending — the astronaut never makes it back to Earth.

And in 1969, just days before Apollo 11 landed on the moon, English singer, songwriter and actor David Bowie released a hit song about "Major Tom," an astronaut who floated into deep space, never making it home.

Today I’m writing a happy story. The NASA astronaut in my family just defied both the movie and the song.

Welcome back to planet Earth, Chris Williams.

NASA CHIEF DECLARES AMERICA 'ABSOLUTELY BACK' IN SPACE RACE, SAYS US WILL BEAT CHINA TO THE MOON

The drive to explore new frontiers is a hallmark of American history, from westward expansion to light bulbs, airplanes and personal computers.

This year, the U.S. sent a mission, Artemis II, to rocket around the moon in preparation for a return to the lunar surface for the first time since Americans Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin stepped on the moon in July 1969.

And this year, I saw my nephew, the grandson of Panamanian immigrants, talking with his fellow astronauts as they sped by his post on the International Space Station.

A few weeks later, Chris’ dad, my brother, Roger, got a Father’s Day greeting as Chris streamed into Trinity Episcopal Church in Washington, D.C. Even more emotional for me was hearing Roger praise his son for going to space and for growing "beyond every expectation."

NEW ARTEMIS II VIDEO SHOWS MOMENT NAVY MEDICAL TEAM OPENED HATCH, WELCOMED ASTRONAUTS

As his uncle, I’ve known Chris since he was a child, wearing a onesie adorned with astronauts and planets. It is hard to get my mind around the idea that he just spent eight months on the International Space Station, completing 3,856 orbits around the Earth at 17,000 miles an hour.

He did spacewalks, floating in space with the American flag on his pressurized spacesuit.

Chris, the highly curious boy, is now a man who successfully returned to Earth on Sunday, July 26.

In a time of national anxiety over war, inflation and polarized politics, Chris is a flesh-and-blood reminder that space travel has the power to inspire awe and renew the American spirit of adventure.

His red, white and blue space adventure is also a powerful retort to the 59% of Americans who told Pew in a May survey ahead of the nation’s 250th birthday that the country’s best days are behind us.

BRET BAIER: WHY AMERICANS STILL BELIEVE OUR BEST DAYS ARE AHEAD, EVEN IN DIVIDED TIMES

Despite all the political controversies orbiting around billionaires Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, America’s leading moguls investing in space exploration, history tells us to focus on achievement. Henry Ford was politically polarizing, but he also revolutionized manufacturing and transportation.

President John F. Kennedy got it right in the 1960s when he said the U.S. mission to land on the moon was an appropriate national goal because it "served to organize and measure the best of our energies and skill."

That is the optimistic message I got as I watched Chris during his time on the space station, including his two spacewalks.

How can I describe watching NASA TV and seeing the eye-popping sight of the son of my brother and his wife, Roger and Ginger, flying through outer space while hanging by a tether from the space station?

He was outside the space station on his last walk for nearly eight hours, working with fellow NASA astronaut Jessica Meir to repair robotic arms.

And in January, a fellow American astronaut on the space station lost his ability to speak and was evacuated with other crew members. Chris was left behind. For a month, he was the only American on the space station.

Part of Chris’s mission was to figure out how to keep astronauts healthy on lengthy space trips as the U.S. works to return to the moon and even send astronauts to Mars.

NASA scientists, including Chris, studied how zero gravity affects the brain and even changes balance and the sense of direction. Chris made himself a subject of study to track how long-term space travel changes human eyes and bone density.

Family alarms went off when NASA ordered Chris and other astronauts to evacuate the space station because of a possible air leak. He took shelter in a small spacecraft.

NASA AT 68: AMERICA MUST LEAD ON THE MOON, MARS AND BEYOND — OR CHINA WILL

This was no movie script. It was genuinely a time of high anxiety for his wife and children in Houston, as well as the whole family, during the two hours before NASA gave the word for him to go back inside.

While in space, Chris’ job was also to inspire young Americans to study math and science and become future space explorers. Chris handled the job with ease. He turned the space station into a fun show for students. They marveled at his ability to turn horizontal and float through the space station like Superman. They wanted to know what he had to eat and how he slept.

Young people in Florida wanted to know the difference between doing scientific research on Earth and in space.

The answer could have been intimidating coming from Chris. He has a physics degree from Stanford and a doctorate from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). And he completed training in medical physics at Harvard Medical School.

NASA'S CHANDRA TELESCOPE REVEALS MILKY WAY'S OUTER REACHES MAY STRETCH FARTHER THAN PREVIOUSLY KNOWN

But he turned the answer into awe-inspiring fun. He called attention to the Velcro strips on his jumpsuit and on the walls. In zero gravity, he explained, every instrument, every tool, every vial, every sample will just float away if not attached.

One of his teaching tricks was to release a bubble of water and watch it float around before he pretended to be Pac-Man and gobbled it out of the air.

He also attracted viral attention with his photography.

The internet started asking about aliens when he posted photos of the West Coast of India showing green, neon lights piercing a dark sky. They turned out to be LED lights used by fishing fleets to attract squid.

His photos of fireworks exploding during Lunar New Year in February, as the space station passed over China, were praised by other astronauts for their astounding beauty.

To me, Chris’ uniquely American life story is also inspiring.

He is the grandson of Black immigrants from Panama, my parents.

In 1958, his grandmother left Colón, Panama, with three children aboard a freighter carrying bananas to Brooklyn, New York. My father also saw opportunities disappearing for Black Panamanians under the racist dictatorship of Arnulfo Arias. It was also time for my older sister to begin high school.

In New York, Chris’ grandmother worked for minimum wage in a Manhattan dress factory — a sweatshop, as they were commonly called — while my father sent what little money he could from Panama.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

A generation later, our family has been blessed beyond measure. We have celebrated children who became lawyers, physicians, business leaders and successful professionals.

On Father’s Day, Chris took time to beam live from space and celebrate his dad and mom in front of the congregation at Washington, D.C.’s Trinity Episcopal Church.

My tears flowed when his dad praised Chris as a son who grew "beyond every expectation." Roger asked that the powers of the universe "bring you home safely." The congregation wished him well "until we see you again."

On Sunday, July 26, Chris landed in Kazakhstan with two Russian cosmonauts. A NASA recovery team was there and returned him to the Johnson Space Center in Houston.

Welcome home, Chris. What an inspiring ride!

item.title: Riley Gaines says Target Center staffer tried to shut down her Sophie Cunningham sign
item.description: Riley Gaines says an arena staffer told her to lower a sign thanking Sophie Cunningham by name while other fans held signs with player names.
item.content:encoded:
Minnesota Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve was permitted to wear a "Trans kids belong" shirt on the sideline during Sunday’s game against the Indiana Fever.

Fans throughout Target Center held signs supporting their favorite WNBA players.

But when Riley Gaines displayed a small sign reading, "Sophie, thank you — a girl mom," an arena staffer tried to make her put it down.

According to Gaines, the staffer told her the problem was that the sign contained Fever guard Sophie Cunningham’s name.

"I checked all the sign policies before I went in there," Gaines told OutKick. "I made sure it was like 11 by 17. That’s the sign size you could have. So, I got a ruler out. You better believe I was measuring it."

TRANS ACTIVISTS HARASS, HURL SLURS AT SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SUPPORTERS BEFORE FEVER GAME IN MINNESOTA

Gaines attended Sunday’s Fever-Lynx game to support Cunningham, who has faced intense criticism since publicly stating that women’s sports should be reserved for women.

Cunningham was loudly booed throughout Indiana’s 108-100 loss in Minneapolis, while Reeve used the game to make her opposing position clear.

ESPN’s broadcast highlighted Reeve’s shirt and encouraged viewers to listen to the Lynx coach’s previous comments on transgender athletes.

Meanwhile, a staffer inside the arena apparently decided Gaines’ simple message of support for Cunningham needed to disappear.

Gaines arrived at Target Center around 11:40 a.m. local time, approximately 20 minutes before tipoff.

She had initially planned to attend a rally outside the arena but remained at her hotel after her personal security team advised her that the situation had become too hostile.

Gaines was not present for a confrontation outside that was was described by some social media users as an "assault." Video reviewed by OutKick showed one person ripping a T-shirt from another person’s hands, but did not appear to show anyone being struck or injured.

As Gaines entered the arena, however, she said a protester stationed near the entrance put a bullhorn near her face, sounded it and shouted at her.

Once inside, the response was mixed.

Gaines said some people directed insults and hostile looks toward her, but many others requested photographs, thanked her, offered fist bumps and quietly expressed support for her position. She said some people even brought copies of Gaines' book into the arena and asked her to sign them.

Around halftime, Gaines said families and young girls formed something resembling a photo line near her seat.

"There were so many people stopping me, asking me for photos, ‘Thank you for doing what you’re doing,’ winks and whispers and fist bumps, people buying me drinks," Gaines said.

At some point during the game, she held up her sign.

"I see an arena staffer, someone who’s on the court wearing the all-black official clothing, who points at me and mouths something," Gaines recalled. "I can’t hear him because he’s so far away, but he appeared to say, ‘Put your sign down.’"

At first, Gaines wasn’t sure the staffer was addressing her. Numerous other people in the arena were holding signs, including signs containing the names of players.

The staffer eventually approached her and repeated the instruction.

"He comes over and he says, ‘You have to take your sign down.’ I’m like, ‘No, I don’t. I checked all the sign policies before I went in there,’" Gaines said.

Gaines asked why her sign was prohibited.

"He said, ‘Well, because it has her name on it. It has Sophie’s name on it, so you can’t have that,’" Gaines recalled.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM FANS ALLEGE STORM PLAYERS, EXEC HECKLED GIRLS DURING GAME OVER SUPPORT OF WOMEN'S SPORTS

The explanation immediately drew objections from other spectators in Gaines’ section.

"My whole section at that point, they were outraged," Gaines said. "They were like, ‘You can’t tell her she can’t have that. There’s a hundred signs right here with people’s names on it. What do you mean she can’t have it?’"

Gaines refused to lower the sign.

"What are you going to do, kick me out?" Gaines recalled thinking. "Go for it."

She said the staffer eventually returned after the game and apologized. Gaines interpreted the apology as a possible indication that he had been directed by someone else to confront her, though she did not know who may have issued that instruction.

Target Center’s published poster and signage policy does not prohibit signs merely because they contain a player’s name.

The policy states:

"As a general rule, posters/signage under 11 x 17 inches are allowed in Target Center, pending individual tour/promoter approval. All posters/signage must be handheld, may not be mounted on sticks or poles, may not be lit or constructed using lighting elements, may not contain offensive language or graphics and may not prevent other guests from seeing the stage/event."

The venue reserves the right to confiscate signs it considers inappropriate and says the policy may change based on requirements for a particular event. But the policy does not state that a sign is prohibited simply because it includes a player’s name.

Gaines said her sign was handheld, smaller than the maximum dimensions and contained no offensive language or graphics. She also said she made certain it complied with the published size restriction before bringing it to the game.

More importantly, Gaines said the staffer didn't tell her that the sign was oversized, offensive, obstructing another fan’s view or violating an event-specific restriction.

CHERYL REEVE SENDS CLEAR MESSAGE TO SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM WITH ‘TRANS KIDS BELONG’ SHIRT DURING FEVER-LYNX GAME

He allegedly told her she could not display it because it contained Cunningham’s name.

OutKick contacted the Minnesota Lynx and asked whether an event-specific signage policy was in place, why Gaines was instructed to lower her sign, whether any policy prohibited Cunningham’s name and whether the direction originated with the Lynx, Target Center, arena security or the WNBA.

The Lynx did not respond to our email.

Cunningham was booed when she entered the game and frequently when she touched the basketball.

But Gaines said the public hostility didn't match many of the private interactions she had with fans inside Target Center and said she believes many people inside the arena agreed with Cunningham but didn't feel comfortable expressing that support openly.

"I absolutely think she had more fans there, or people who at least support her sentiment, than are willing to admit," Gaines said.

Cunningham eventually made a 3-pointer late in the third quarter and received a noticeable cheer despite playing for the visiting team.

Gaines viewed that reaction as another sign that the loudest people in the arena didn't necessarily represent everyone in attendance.

After the game ended, Cunningham came out to meet Gaines near the tunnel.

Most of the players had already left the court, but Gaines said several young girls remained nearby calling Cunningham’s name.

Cunningham spent approximately 15 minutes with Gaines and posed for a photograph while holding the same sign the arena staffer had attempted to make Gaines lower.

Gaines described Cunningham as completely unshaken by the hostile reception.

According to Gaines, Cunningham said she knew her position was right and remained confident that she could defend it intellectually and morally. Because of that confidence, Cunningham said the reaction did not bother her.

While the loudest voices inside Target Center spent the afternoon condemning Cunningham, young girls waited near the tunnel chanting her name. Fans quietly approached Gaines to thank her. And Cunningham came back out after the loss to greet them.

The arena allowed Reeve to promote her message from the sideline. Fans were free to boo Cunningham every time she touched the ball. But when Gaines held up a small sign thanking Cunningham, a staffer told her it had to come down because it contained the player’s name.

Gaines refused.

By the end of the afternoon, Cunningham was holding the sign herself.

item.title: King Charles makes risky move toward Prince Harry as Prince William 'remains wary': experts
item.description: King Charles reportedly plans to offer Prince Harry a room at Buckingham Palace during his September visit, but experts say Prince William is wary.
item.content:encoded:
Prince Harry's return to the United Kingdom could be King Charles' biggest gamble yet — and Prince William may not like it.

The claim was made by multiple royal experts who spoke to Fox News Digital following reports that the Duke of Sussex is expected to visit the U.K. in September. The Sun reported that the monarch plans to offer his younger son a room at Buckingham Palace in London during his stay.

Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace and Archewell, which oversees the offices of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, for comment.

KING CHARLES SENDS 'DEFIANCE' MESSAGE TO PRINCE WILLIAM WITH BUCKINGHAM PALACE ROOM OFFER TO HARRY: EXPERT

"Prince Harry has been invited to stay at Buckingham Palace to coincide with the annual WellChild Awards, which he attends each year," British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital. "This is perceived as an olive branch by King Charles to slowly rebuild their relationship. However, will Prince Harry accept the invitation? There are murmurs that he has accepted it. Time will tell."

"My sources say staff at Buckingham Palace are against Harry staying," Chard said. "They feel immensely betrayed by Harry's explosive claims against the royal family. Also, my sources say there has been no hint of contrition from the Sussexes. People are not going to forget that they hurled the royal family under the bus, creating lasting damage to the crown. Many wonder why King Charles is appeasing Harry."

The olive branch came after the Sussexes had a rare reunion with Charles during their visit to the U.K. in July. The private meeting, which took place at Charles' country estate, Highgrove House, marked the first time the king had seen his grandchildren, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, since 2022.

WATCH: PRINCE WILLIAM UNLIKELY TO RECONCILE WITH PRINCE HARRY SOON: EXPERT

Harry's recent visit to the U.K. was marked by problems.

After reports that the prince would visit his home country with his family, the British government declined his request for police protection outside royal residences, prompting him to travel alone on July 6.

The Sussexes lost their taxpayer-funded security after they stepped back as senior working royals. Harry was later denied the restoration of that security by the Executive Committee for the Protection of Royalty and Public Figures (RAVEC).

The couple previously lived at Nottingham Cottage on the grounds of Kensington Palace in London before moving to Frogmore Cottage in Windsor shortly before Archie was born in 2019. After they stepped back as working royals in 2020 and relocated to California, the Sussexes were asked to vacate Frogmore Cottage.

People magazine reported that ahead of Harry's trip, his team spent several days exploring ways to make the visit safe through enhanced private security arrangements. Palace sources told the outlet Harry initially declined an invitation to stay at a royal residence before later accepting it.

Harry's spokesperson told the outlet that an offer for the Duke of Sussex to stay at Buckingham Palace during his London visit was withdrawn after he had formally accepted it. Palace sources, however, disputed that account, saying Harry failed to respond by the deadline and that his later acceptance came only after arrangements could no longer be made.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

A source close to the Sussexes told the outlet that, behind the scenes, the drama surrounding the visit was "quite stressful."

"What was billed as a big homecoming ... turned into a nightmare," Russell Myers, author of "William & Catherine," told the outlet. "It was further evidence of the fractiousness of Harry's relationship with the institution."

Katie Nicholl, Vanity Fair's royal correspondent, reported that, according to sources, "not even the Prince and Princess of Wales were made aware" that a meeting would take place on July 10 between the Sussexes and the king.

She also reported that Charles, "who has sworn his youngest son and daughter-in-law to secrecy," insisted that nothing about their July 10 meeting be leaked. Only palace aides were permitted to confirm the reunion had taken place after the Sussexes left Highgrove House without being seen.

Royal experts told Fox News Digital that while Charles is open to reconciling with his younger son and reconnecting with his California-based grandchildren, not everyone is welcoming the Sussexes with open arms. 

Prince William is said to remain wary of his estranged brother, many of them shared. According to the experts, the brothers have not spoken since 2022, when their grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II, died.

"King Charles, from all indications and all feedback from courtiers, obviously wants to maintain an open dialogue and ongoing relationship with his 'dear boy,'" British royals expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital. "Prince William, meanwhile, remains wary and won't want Harry at the palace. However, it's better that Harry stays at Buckingham Palace than in Windsor, which is too close to William and his family."

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

If Charles hopes to bring Harry back into the royal fold, he'll first need the blessing of the future king, royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams said.

"The attitude of the Waleses, since they are the monarchy's future, is pivotal," Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital. "And with good reason, they don't trust the Sussexes. King Charles' approach could prove incendiary."

Still, Chard believes Charles appears willing to risk fresh royal tensions in pursuit of something he's long wanted: reconciliation with Harry.

"Don't get me wrong, reconciliation within the British royal family would be good as it makes the monarchy stronger," Chard said. "However, why invite Harry to Buckingham Palace, the iconic royal residence that's the administrative heart of the monarchy? Harry is no longer a working royal and shouldn't be offered a room at Buckingham Palace."

"I guess the optics of inviting Harry to Buckingham Palace are seen as a goodwill gesture, easing tensions with small steps forward, peace-wise," Chard said. "It also skates over the endless divide within the family."

Chard previously told Fox News Digital that William is known for being stubborn behind palace doors and isn't one to forgive easily.

"William believes the monarchy must be seen to do the right thing, even when it's painful. From what I understand, he felt his father didn't handle that firmly enough. He also believes in protecting it by drawing hard lines. But he's not the king yet."

During part of their U.K. visit, the Sussexes stayed at Althorp, Princess Diana's ancestral home, where they were hosted by Harry's uncle, Earl Charles Spencer. It was there that Archie and Lilibet learned more about their grandmother, who died when Harry was 12, according to People.

Meghan later shared photos of Harry and their children at the estate on Instagram.

Fordwich previously told Fox News Digital that William was likely "livid" over the photos.

"Not only is Prince William likely to be livid regarding the commercialization of Althorp in such a tacky, tasteless media post, but it'll fuel his disgust, so he [would] thwart any major re-entry," she said. "Likewise, Camilla, courtiers, palace aides, security officials and other institutional gatekeepers who are duty-bound to protect the monarchy will all do their utmost to thwart Meghan and Harry's attempts."

item.title: Trump v. Smithsonian: A timeline of how the White House fight over 'woke' history unfolded
item.description: Trump's executive orders target the Smithsonian Institution, arguing exhibits prioritize decolonization and DEI over patriotic American history.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump's effort to root out what his administration calls "woke" ideology at the Smithsonian has grown into one of the most extensive White House reviews of the institution in decades.

The Smithsonian oversees 21 museums, the National Zoo and nearly 157 million objects and specimens while receiving more than $1 billion annually in federal funding outside of private-side dollars.

The administration's campaign has placed the taxpayer-supported institution at the center of a broader debate over patriotism, historical interpretation and the role of federally funded cultural institutions amid a growing divide over how people view and retell America's story.

GOP LAWMAKER DEMANDS ANSWERS AFTER SMITHSONIAN CHIEF URGED MOVING BEYOND 'AMERICA FIRST MENTALITY'

Over the past 16 months, the administration has examined museum exhibits, educational programming, internal records and leadership statements, issued multiple document requests, interviewed curators and conducted on-site museum walkthroughs.

The effort culminated in a 162-page White House report recommending sweeping reforms and announcing new executive actions aimed at implementing those recommendations.

Here's a timeline of the major developments.

Trump signed an executive order titled "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History" two months into his second term. The order argues that federal cultural institutions, including the Smithsonian, have promoted "divisive" ideological narratives.

The executive action directs the Trump administration to restore what it describes as a more patriotic presentation of American history. And it tasks the White House Domestic Policy Council and Vice President JD Vance, in his role as a Smithsonian Regent, with reviewing Smithsonian exhibits and programs.

Following Trump's executive order, the White House Domestic Policy Council kicked-off an investigation of the Smithsonian, focusing primarily on the National Museum of American History.

Officials reviewed exhibits, educational materials, strategic plans, leadership speeches, museum programming and public statements. During that review, the council documented examples they argue prioritize divisive ideological narratives over a so-called patriotic telling of American history.

White House officials sent Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch a letter formally launching the review ordered by Trump.

The letter directs the institution to turn over exhibition plans, educational materials, internal policies and other records while outlining a review of eight Smithsonian museums to ensure exhibits "celebrate American exceptionalism" and remove what the administration calls divisive narratives.

It also sets deadlines for document production, curator interviews and on-site reviews, with museums instructed to begin revising public-facing content within 120 days.

The White House criticizes the museum for holding no special Independence Day programming in 2025 despite being open on July 4, discontinuing its traditional Flag Day ceremonies, and planning 250th anniversary exhibits and events.

According to the administration, those 250 installations emphasize flaws of the United States while giving insufficient attention to the Founders, the Declaration of Independence and the American Revolution.

The White House tells Smithsonian Secretary Bunch in a letter that the institution has failed to provide most of the records requested during its review.

Among other things, the review requested exhibition plans, curatorial documents and governance materials be turned over.

At this time, the administration gives the Smithsonian until Jan. 13, 2026, to produce the requested records. It also reminds the institution that federal funding must be used in a manner consistent with Trump's "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History" executive order.

White House investigators complete on-site walkthroughs of Smithsonian museums. During the visits, they reviewed exhibits, educational materials, digital content and internal planning documents as well as interviewed museum staff as part of the administration's review.

SMITHSONIAN'S NATIONAL MUSEUM OF AMERICAN HISTORY PROMOTES 'EXTREME POLITICAL ACTIVISM,' WH REPORT ALLEGES

Investigators found during those visits exhibits that they argue emphasized restorative history, decolonization, immigration activism, DEI initiatives and social justice. Meanwhile, it claimed that the institution was downplaying America's Founders, the nation's achievements and patriotic themes.

The report ultimately concludes the Smithsonian project has undergone a significant shift away from its original mission, arguing exhibits increasingly emphasize social justice activism and ideological narratives rather than focus on America's founding principles and national achievements.

The museum debuts its signature exhibition commemorating America's 250th anniversary, featuring 250 objects from its collection, including Thomas Jefferson's writing desk, George Washington's uniform and the Star-Spangled Banner.

The White House said just two months before the country's 250th celebration that the exhibition repackages existing displays rather than creating a new founding-era exhibit. It also criticized the installation for failing to meaningfully celebrate America's Founders, the Declaration of Independence or the American Revolution during the nation's 250th birthday.

The Trump administration also said the exhibit's promotional materials and programming downplayed patriotic themes and national symbols.

The White House Domestic Policy Council releases its 162-page "Saving America's Story" report, concluding that the National Museum of American History has undergone "ideological capture."

The report recommends removing what it describes as political activism from museum exhibits and restoring displays that emphasize America's founding principles, national achievements and patriotic history. It says the findings stem from the Smithsonian review ordered by Trump's March 2025 executive order.

The expansive report included images of exhibits, images of exhibits and placards, as well as curators and leaders of the museum.

It spent much of the report focusing on how the museum classified and portrayed illegal migration in its exhibits.

Hours after the report's release, Trump signs the "Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution" executive order, directing the Interior Department, Office of Management and Budget (OMB), General Services Administrator (GSA) and the White House Domestic Policy Council to use available authorities to encourage the Smithsonian to address the report's findings.

TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY

Trump's order also instructs the National Park Service (NPS) to install temporary signs outside the National Museum of American History directing visitors to the report and describing the administration's concerns with the museum's presentation of American history.

The administration says its effort is intended to restore a more patriotic presentation of American history at the Smithsonian. The institution, meanwhile, has long said its mission is to preserve and present the nation's history through scholarship, research and public education, setting the stage for continued debate over how America's story should be told.

The Smithsonian did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
